highlight.title: Automation-Migration Interface: How AI Reshapes Migrant Labour Market Integration
highlight.summary: A new preprint introduces the concept of the 'Automation-Migration Interface,' arguing that technological change is restructuring the dual labour market in ways that disproportionately expose migrant workers to displacement risk. The study builds on dual labour market theory to show that automation and migration pressures interact, compounding integration challenges for foreign-born workers. This has direct implications for understanding overall workforce displacement patterns across skill and demographic segments. (Grabowska et al., 2026)

highlight.title: Replacement vs. Augmentation: Student and Faculty Views on AI's Labor Market Impact
highlight.summary: A peer-reviewed study surveying Romanian students and faculty finds deeply divided views on whether AI will replace or merely augment human workers, with younger respondents more likely to anticipate augmentation while faculty express greater displacement concern. The research highlights that perceptions of AI's labor market role vary substantially by educational level and domain, with white-collar professional roles seen as most at risk. These attitudes are shaping how institutions prepare graduates for an AI-transformed workforce. (Aivaz, Teodorescu & Radu, 2026)

highlight.title: AI Agents Autonomously Execute High Energy Physics Experiments with Minimal Expert Input
highlight.summary: Researchers demonstrate that LLM-based AI agents using Claude can autonomously carry out substantial portions of a high-energy physics analysis pipeline—including data processing and result interpretation—with minimal expert-curated guidance. This marks a significant milestone in agentic AI adoption within highly specialized scientific workflows, suggesting accelerating displacement of expert-level technical labor in research settings. The findings raise urgent questions about the future role of domain specialists in AI-augmented scientific environments. (Moreno et al., 2026)

highlight.title: Six-Agent AI System Replaces Costly Cybersecurity Risk Assessments for Small Organizations
highlight.summary: A multi-agent AI architecture is shown to replicate NIST CSF-aligned cybersecurity risk assessments—engagements that typically cost $15,000 and take weeks—at a fraction of the cost and time. Each of the six agents specializes in a distinct assessment domain, collectively matching the output of scarce human practitioners. This case study exemplifies how agentic AI is beginning to automate high-skill, high-cost professional services, with material implications for wage premiums in technical consulting roles. (Gupta et al., 2026)

highlight.title: Human-AI Orchestration in Software Delivery: Field Study Across Three Modernization Programs
highlight.summary: A longitudinal retrospective field study of the Chiron industrial platform examines how coordinating human and AI agents across four software delivery stages impacts team-level productivity and role boundaries in real software modernization programs. The study finds that AI orchestration meaningfully alters task allocation, with some human roles narrowing in scope as agents absorb routine delivery work. This is one of the first team-level (rather than individual task-level) empirical assessments of AI's effects on software engineering labor. (Armesto & Kolb, 2026)
